The berries contain high levels of vitamins A, C; minerals such as phosphorous, magnesium, calcium, potassium and iron as well as essential fatty acids and bioflavonoids. (The lycopene content in the autumn olive fruit is 17 times higher than that in a tomato.) Other carotenoids the berries contain are B-carotene, phytoene, and a- and b-cryptoxanthin. The fruit also contains malic acid like the crab apple and when fully ripe has glucose and fructose present. The berries can be frozen and used later.

Traditional Medicine Uses

The flowers are used as a cardiac tonic and are astringing and stimulating. The seeds are said to be good for coughs, and the oil from the seeds is used to treat afflictions of the lungs. The berries can be dried and stored to use in fruit teas or tisanes. The flowers can also be made into a tisane with the leaves. description:
For years, I've seen the sign for the Alexandria Cemetery and wondered if it would be a nice place to walk. It is. There are several acres of land and meadows along the back of the property, full of milkweeds (*A. tuberosa* and *A. syriaca*) and dogbane (*Apocynum cannabinum*).

A thin strip of woods separates the cemetery from adjoining properties, and unfortunately, many of the woody plants growing there are invasives. I saw some Callery Pear, plenty of Amur Honeysuckle, and this huge Autumn Olive.

The Autumn Olive shrub was about the size of a flowering dogwood tree and covered in fruit. These seem to fruit irregularly, so I take this as a sign of an impending mast year.

The scales that cover the fruit and foliage are a unique trait of the Elaeagnaceae.

description: Fall hike at the Kenton County Conservation District's Morning View Heritage Area and the invasives were out in force, sadly. We hiked a loop through oak-hickory-beech woods and then through more open land heading back. This was done by following the Kreissl Trail through the woods and then cutting over to the parking area on the Dickerson Trail. We did see some lovely native plants as well, but they seemed outnumbered by boisterously fruiting invasives such as Berberis thunbergii, Lonicera japonica and L. maackii, and Ligustrum. There was fruiting Autum Olive all along the initial segment of the Kreissl Trail, heading away from the parking area. I saw several more shrubs of this species as we hiked further. I ate several of the fruits and though scaly, they had a pleasant sweet-tart flavor, almost like a plum.
